Edit: a good app for approximating sunrise/sunset. I have used multiple different sunrise/sunset apps, and Aplenglow is by far the best one. I can honestly say, that without an ounce of doubt, that if this app says that it’ll be a good sunset, then it will absolutely be a good one. Since I travel extensively for my job, I have used this app to try and find out when there will be a beautiful sunset that I can photograph, and share it with my wife so that we can “share” the experience via FaceTime. Thanks to this app, when I was working out at North Island Naval Air Station in San Diego, I was able to choose the right day to head out to Sunset Cliffs National Park and share a West Coast Sunset with my wife in Florida. I HIGHLY recommend this app for anyone trying to track the sunrise/sunset…  Addendum: I’ve dropped my rating by one star due to some instances of extreme inaccuracy. Usually the erroneous percentages are on days when the forecast is “poor” or “fair,” but there have also been a couple times when a “good” or “great” sunrise/sunset ended up being mediocre at best. That said, the initial review still stands, as MORE OFTEN THAN NOT, the forecast is relatively accurate. I have read other reviews and comments from the developer, that point out the fact that the local weather forecast is not always accurate, which is a fair statement. I do wonder though, why I have read replies from the developer that says he’s been working on improvements and attempting to work with local news outlets (and other methods of making this app better) that have read the same way for two years of reviews…I have to wonder if there have been any actual improvement updates…regardless, this app is one of the best for this particular purpose

Polished and well-supported app, incredibly responsive developer. Due to days of rain/clouds in my location, I haven’t yet been able to test the accuracy of the forecasts, but in anticipation of eventually seeing the sun again, I’ve poked around in the app and really love how it’s laid out. Intuitive and easy to use, with some really excellent features. I love the 4-day forecast option, as well as the notification options. I really like seeing all the times laid out for first and last light, golden hour and blue hour, and of course, sunrise and sunset. It’s a really good-looking app with more functionality than you’re going to find on, say, sunsetwx.com, which is what I’ve used for years.  Communication with the developer is super-easy with multiple email links to provide feedback, and I had an opportunity to use this when I couldn’t get “Restore Purchase” to work and enable me to use the app on all my devices. I emailed my feedback and had a friendly, personalized response within hours saying he’d reported the bug and offering a workaround, and asking me to let him know if the workaround didn’t fix my issue (it did). If you have an Apple Watch, the Watch app is just the thing, with really intuitive displays and functionality, by the way. I think I may love the Watch app even more than I do the phone/iPad app.  I recognize that no sunset/sunrise prediction can be 100% accurate every time, any more than a weather forecast will be. Those of us chasing light should know the factors that create a great sunrise or sunset and consider this app, or sunsetwx, or any other prediction app to be a “rule of thumb” kind of general guide. This one is polished and offers exceptional functionality across multiple devices, and you can’t beat the responsiveness of the developer! I find the $24.95 lifetime cost of this app (the most economical way to support this developer) to be entirely worth it.

Consistently wrong or useless. I have been using this app for months, and what’s most striking is that it’s consistently wrong, or proving a useless metric.   It uses a zero to 100% scale, and then also uses that scale to categorize the sunset’s quality. So tonight it predicted 27.5%, and had a FAIR categorization. Most often, it predicts somewhere between 47% and 52%. I can’t recall what that corresponds to as a categorized quality, something like MODERATE.  Now the first question this raises is: what does this percentage even mean? Is it a confidence, like when there’s a 40% chance of rain? If so, tonight’s 27.5% means a 27.5% confidence that the sunset will be FAIR? I don’t think that’s what it’s supposed to indicate, because the whatever this percentage is supposed to correspond to, as it goes up, so does the quality categorization, i.e.: they’re the same thing. One is simply a continuous scale and the other is a categorical scale.   So what do these percentages mean? I don’t know, but I guess it leaves the concept that this is just a zero to 100% scale of quality, and the confidence in that prediction is… 100%? That’s a bad way to go about predictions, but if that’s how it works, then having a near-always 47% to 52% prediction is roughly as useful as a coin toss.   So tonight, the sunset was pretty good. If I were going to rate it on a zero to 100% scale of quality, I’d probably give it a 62-67%.   Now I pull out the app, mostly to laugh at what it’s predicted and try to take note of how wrong or useless it was.   *I would give this one star only, but statistical analysis of crowd ratings usually heavily discounts 1 and 5 because people almost always use those ratings.

Loyalty Lost: From Decade-Long Advocate to Frustrated Customer. I am writing this review as someone who was once Chatbooks' biggest fan and very loyal customer. I maintained multiple feeds and printed them regularly and consistently. My history with this company is extensive. Remember the 100 club? I wore it proudly.  Unfortunately, everything has changed by 2025. The application is now slow, glitchy, and spontaneously crashes, turning what used to be a fun, simple process into a frustrating chore. The print quality of their books has reduced significantly. The new business model feels like a forced cash-grab. It hooks you into subscriptions and prevents you from making books on your own time. The issue with the “credits” system is awful: I was charged hundreds of dollars in “credits” only to have them expire after 12 months. I received the complete runaround when trying to address this financial loss. When attempting to get assistance, customer service is a flop. It is primarily AI-based, and when you finally "chat" with a human, they seem indifferent and entirely unhelpful. The ultimate betrayal of my decade-long loyalty is being denied access to my older books and feeds—the very content I invested so much time and money creating. I was told I must now pay and subscribe just to view the books I paid for and printed. I was told I "opted into a new billing system,” which I do not believe I did, nor would I have, knowing the access to past books would be gone. At this point, I am entirely frustrated with Chatbooks. My loyalty has been ignored, my funds have been confiscated through expired credits, and my data is being held hostage. The service has been unreliable, the quality is poor, and customer support doesn't care. I strongly warn potential new customers: do not invest your cherished memories here.

Cosmos Feature Suggestion: Smarter Import / Board Updating. I’d love to suggest an improvement to the import feature in Cosmos, because I think it has the potential to become one of the app’s most useful tools.  Right now, importing a folder or file into a board seems to treat every import as a completely new upload. This works fine the first time, but it becomes messy when importing the same folder again, especially if it comes from something like Pinterest and already has multiple sections inside it. Instead of recognizing what already exists, Cosmos can create duplicate sections or re-import things that are already on the board.  Since the import feature is extremely useful, I think it would be even stronger if it worked more like an update or sync system.  For example, if I import a folder into an existing board, Cosmos could check whether that board already has sections with the same names. If those sections already exist, the app could merge into them instead of creating duplicates. Then, if certain files or images are already present, Cosmos could recognize them and skip them rather than importing them again.  I’m not sure what the technical solution would be, but maybe each file could have some kind of unique identifier, metadata, image fingerprint, or code that lets the system tell whether it has already been imported. That way, Cosmos could avoid duplicates even if the same folder is imported more than once.  A smarter import system could include things like:  * Merge with existing sections * Skip duplicate files automatically * Detect when the same folder has already been imported * Update an existing board instead of creating repeat sections * Show an import preview before confirming * Let users choose between “import as new” and “update existing board”  This would make the import feature much more reliable and streamlined, especially for people using Cosmos to organize large moodboards, Pinterest exports, reference folders, or visual archives.  Overall, I think the import tool is already a very valuable feature. It just needs a smarter way to recognize what is already inside a board so users can keep building on their collections without accidentally creating clutter.

But it’s hard to give it a chance when I feel like it’s not giving *me* a chance.   After several hours of actively trying to curate my feed, my FYP is still predominantly beige rocks. Some of them are artsy rocks. I can appreciate Noguchi or Brancusi as much as anyone! Others just seem to be… rocks. And, no matter what I do to convince my algorithm that I’m just not that into rocks, I still get rocks.   I read a review from someone who was disappointed by the lack of NASCAR and NFL content on the app. The developer wrote that the app wasn’t for people who were interested in NASCAR or the NFL. I think that gets at one major problem. The developers seem to have a very narrow-minded vision of who the app is for - which does the app a disservice. Sure, it’s supposed to be for creatives. But creativity needs diversity to flourish. Who says creatives can’t draw inspiration from Isamu Noguchi *and* the NFL?  There’s another issue with this app. One of my biggest gripes with Pinterest is its rampant sourcing problem. It’s often hard to find the original artist or creator behind an image.   I would’ve thought that a platform targeted towards creatives would be better about giving credit. Cosmos is *actively worse.* Most of the images are uncredited, and there’s no way to comment or add context to an existing image to help other people find the source. If I’m getting pictures of rocks, at least give me a little more info! What makes the rock special? Is it part of an art piece? If so, who’s the artist?  The app has potential, but right now it’s just pretty pictures without context or credit. If you want pretty pictures without context or credit, you might as well use AI.

Good! VSCO meets Pinterest. Lovely app with potential! I am migrating my photos from Pinterest to back them up and although Cosmos isn’t as seamless and enjoyable (yet) as Pinterest, it is a great alternative. However, I changed my 5 stars to 3 because saves are limited to a certain amount, which is a pretty easy threshold to surpass. This will be a lengthy review including features unique to Cosmos, features I love, improvements, and features to add. I know it is very long but I wanted to be as informative and helpful as possible.  Features unique to Cosmos: (1) the Canvas feature; I can see my “elements” (photos) in a “cluster” (board), zoom out, also click on an individual photo to go to the source. (2) I can see/access the cluster an individual saved the image to through “connections”. (3) Search by color; self-explanatory :)  Intuitive features I love: (1) the dashboard at the bottom; the home, search, create, activity, and profile are ideally placed. (2) long-pressing a photo; this allows me to reorder, save to another cluster, and delete with ease.  And lastly… Some improvements: (1) Lag; app starts to lag when dragging an element to reorder it inside of the cluster once you move past the end of the page. (2) Algorithm; algorithm doesn’t seem to take into account ALL of the elements you have saved but rather just the last few (which usually is the same set of things e.g. ocean photos, flowers) which is frustrating. (3) Limited saves on Free Plan; this would force me to get Premium. I am happy to pay to support the creators and keep Cosmos add-free, HOWEVER the only option is Premium ($72/year) which is an absurd and unjustifiable amount.  Features to add: (1) Sub-section within a Cluster; I absolutely loved using this feature in Pinterest to streamline my space/time. (2) Light-mode; there are no mode options as the “default” is technically the app itself. I would love a light-mode to brighten it up!  (3) Tiered pricing; In addition to established creatives, a lot of young users are amongst the target audience. We do not have disposable income so tiered pricing could ultimately benefit Cosmos. Flag and reject suffers from the lack of a side-by-side comparison feature – without it, triaging pics is slow going and nowhere near as efficient as described, especially for snappers who rely on burst mode (eg nature or sports). As for the curves (described in marketing materials as the “heart and soul” of Darkroom), this was pretty revelatory at first, but very quickly grew tiresome due to the lack of a left-handed interface. I primarily triage and edit pics on an iPad Pro with an Apple Pencil, and I’m left-handed. Having to reach across the image and obscure it to make edits makes the whole process annoying enough when you’re using your hand to make inputs, but with an Apple Pencil it’s pretty much unusable. Besides having to move my hand to actually see the changes I was making, my palm kept contacting the screen by accident, resulting in spurious inputs. I emailed the developer to ask about a left-handed interface and was told that this was something they were seriously considering, although it would require a lot of work. After my subscription had run for a year with no sign of a left-handed option, I cancelled – I just wasn’t using the app enough, because it made me hate editing my photos, and a hobby is meant to be enjoyable. Fast forward to today and Darkroom still doesn’t have a left-handed interface, despite the app being 10 years old. Instead they continue to churn out custom app icons, the most useless feature imaginable. I’m actually surprised and disappointed that Apple gave this app an award, since left-handed utility is an important accessibility issue. Thankfully I recently discovered Nitro, which besides being an exceptional triage and editing tool (with side-by-side comparisons), also has a left-handed interface. To the folk at Bergen: consider the message you’re sending to users when you lock them out of “the heart and soul” of your app. It’ll take a while for you to regain the trust of people you neglect for no good reason.

Superb Photo editor marred by dangerous bugs. I love the interface and I do not want to stop using it: It's great and intuitive to use. I'm giving 4* at the moment, not 5* mainly because of a number of potentially dangerous bugs, which might cause loss of edits or edits applied or photos being wrongly discarded.  Everything you can do with Apple's editor you can do with this App, but better, faster and with more accurate edits. It is also excellent for curation because (unlike Apple) it can show a photos details, filesize and resolution etc. There are also things in this app that can't be done with the Apple photo editor. There's a useful mask set and you can batch edit/crop/rotate a set of photos.  The 2 things that put me off is the moment are:  The appalling inconsistency between photo-edited/exported flags in the edit-screen-side-photo-strip and in the thumbnail flags on the library view.  Inconsistent and dangerous photo views and photo details shown in the edit screen. For instance, moving from one photo to the next by repeatedly flicking-right/left may not move the photo shown properly in the photo strip, which has a dangerous impact on the displayed photo status. Further, using the photo strip to move from photo to photo by tapping on it may not result in the correct photo or details being shown. This may not be apparent, if you have a lot of very similar photos such as burst mode sequences or other photo sets, for instance. You can end up applying the wrong edits to the wrong photo.  In addition to the above there has been a long standing bug whereby if a photo is deleted from the photo edit screen, the photo that is shown correctly is the next photo after the one deleted, but the details of the deleted photo are shown instead of the correct next photo details. This might be the key to understanding why the flag/film-strip/photo-displayed results are inconsistent on the edit screen. It seems there might be an issue for a photo, especially after changes have been made to the previous photo.  I've got plenty more bugs like this to notify, and I would do so more methodically, if only I was on the latest iPadOS version. You have been warned.  I have been known to write code professionally myself though not on this platform and I'm retired. If I were part of Darkroom's development team, I would be suggesting an urgent review of the consistency of the photo movement and edit/export flags shown code on the edit screen.   In fairness to the Darkroom team, it may be that iPadOS is misreporting details and the fault is not with the Darkroom code.   I'm using this app on an iPad mini at iPadOS 14.8.1. I might find if I upgraded to iPadOS 15.7.1 these issues would disappear, but I am not in a position to do this uograde yet.  My files are either jpg or png, so I'm not a professional photographer either, but I do have 1,000s of photos. It is a testament to the basic design of this app that a small iPad device, with limited RAM can achieve acceptable results at all. But, please team, do urgently review your photo selection and flag setting code.

Curvetastic!. Darkroom simply has the best, smoothest, quickest and most intuitive curve editor I have used on a small device. You are not able to offset the curves, effectively altering what is considered shadow or highlights but having that level of control on a small screen using only your thumb can be fiddly as I've found in some other Apps.  Darkroom doesn't come with a plethora of extra features (some basic masking, would be a bonus) but between the curve editor and the hue, saturation and luminance slider controls, you are able to quickly create beautiful grades.   The app is also fast, you don't have to import an image first before you start grading, open the app and away you go.   The extra filters you can purchase are nice and serve as a great start point for grading your footage as you can see and edit the grade effect, meaning you can quickly learn how to create your own grade presets.  I also really appreciate the location of all the controls. Top of the screen is your image, bottom of the screen are your editing controls. This is an app that's been designed from the ground up to be used on a small device, is quick and not bloated with unnecessary extras. Exploring Lightroom Alternatives For Various Reasons.... To give a little context of my review, I have had a full CC suite subscription for going on 4 years and have owned Photoshop & lightroom full licenses since 2002, rarely the most recent version, but rarely older than 5 years as well. That said, I haven't explored much else available for processing or "digitally developing" my RAW files and I was curious to discover what was out there for free, at an enthusiast's price range, and at the highest level for full-time professional photographers, just to see if there was anything I could use to improve my control, workflow, or even save me money. I found that most software was either incredibly underwhelming, offering little more than the most basic exposure & color tools OR the functions were vast but the quality of adjustments was rough or just unnatural - posterized, really - in fact, despite some aspects of ACDSee I really liked, the absolute deal breaker is the adjustment & output quality - the program does not do well with carrying out the adjustments that Lightroom would be capable of rendering perfectly naturally, subtly, & accurately - which, really, the failure to reliably produce images with natural, smooth tonality, & saturation gradations, while also giving at least adequate features to develop RAW respectably is really was this program offers. That is not to be underappreciated. The file rendering using this program is natural & adjustments don't come at the cost of tonal gradation, nor do they seem to sharpen or blur the edges...  If you need an inexpensive digital developing program - really, if you are shooting in RAW (or have the ability to) and want to take your photos to the next level but aren't ready to spring for the creative suite by Adobe, this is the best option you have that I have seen after going through a dozen or so trials. There are other notable options, but this is certainly easy to use and complete in terms of adjustments & overall features. It offers what you really need and really nothing more - at least 90% of your photos can be processed to a professional standard - assuming the RAWs aren't terribly underexposed or require drastic local adjustments - I have sold multiple 12x18" prints, 50MP TIFFs, & 20MB JPGs to art collectors, online photography enthusiast "zines", and stock platforms like shutterstock using only this program for all of the digital development & had absolutely no problem selling them - honestly, it's hard to know what is lightroom & what i used darkroom to develop; this type of program can help make a better photographer out of those spending too much time with their RAWS already in programs like photoshop & lightroom, and you really should be composing & exposing well enough to rarely need much more than what this offers unless you are shooting under a really highly demanding lighting condition(s), erratic, fast motion, or portraits requiring blemish removal or other local tools like healing, or graduated adjustments for shooting into sunrise/sunset, or bringing back detail in the moon by local exposure adjustments or using a burn/dodge to brighten night scenes while retaining detail in the highlights like the moon or a partially illuminated scene... or if you are trying to produce a highly nuanced, stylized "look", although the split toning & color wheel features can offer some pretty decent color control for that polished, 'cinema' or the old proprietary c41 color "look", like kodachrome or the early polaroid instant filmstock color processing/look - you can push image color pretty far using the color wheels and LRGB curves, sat/vib/temp/tint... My only complaint is the lack of clarity/haze-dehaze/sharpening threshold options. this is a lot longer than it should have been, but, suffice to say, this is the only program I am still using after a month other than DPP by Canon (another discovery I made while trying these other apps out), which is valuable because it has outstanding noise reduction & basic exposure control, though it is best to export to DNG & avoid pushing too hard in DPP, if it needs more than a "10.5"-ish on the noise reduction sliders in DPP, the rest of the denoising is best in Lightroom... Whereas this program shines for producing JPGs for social media from hi-res RAWS quickly, reliably, and without intolerable compression artifacting endemic to so many resized, HIGH-RES JPG images, especially viewed on a browser on a phone.... ooof... but ya, I have been using this for a lot of the JPG images I am posting on social media, sites, and for the stock image sites - because I mostly work in .CR3, DNG, & 16-BIT TIFF for 16-bit print output, I work in the printer profile color space more often than not, & found that a simple RAW-JPG conversion is often disasterous, but this program puts out good results in JPG at reduced resolutions without thumbnail artefacting or unsightly over-sharpening.... and, if you wanted to use to for producing high quality prints from RAW or TIFF, i am sure it would do a fine job, as I have made a good half dozen prints using this software and was pleased - a rare phenomenon, i am very particular regarding my prints. hope this helps.

Darkroom has been the last piece of the puzzle to let me have the tools I want and work completely Adobe free.  Things are always changing in the world of software development and photo/video editing workflow, but my killer combo right now is Darkroom (for raw processing), Hash Photos or Slidebox (for an iCloud Photo based organization system similar to Bridge/Lightroom) and Affinity Photo (as a Photoshop alternative when I decide there is some heavy lifting retouch work to be done).  I appreciate Darkroom’s toolset and really well executed UI. I make pretty liberal use of the flagging feature (similar to LR/Bridge) for my initial photo cull. The Curves tool crushes Lightroom mobile, although I’d love to see this to be expanded to make it easier to adjust each of the RGB channels individually.   The only thing I can think of as really missing here is a pincushion/lens distortion correction tool. All of the raw processors I’m aware of (and I’ve used them all) these days, at a minimum, have a tool for manually dialing out lens distortion that comes from wide angle lenses - but most of them also have an internal library of lens distortion profiles to automatically correct the distortion based on the lens when it’s passed to the raw file via metadata.  At the moment, if I’ve got lens distortions to correct it means I need to move over to Affintiy Photo - which isn’t the end of the world, but a minor annoyance if that’s the only non-raw correction that needs to be made. I find myself doing it frequently as of late though because I’ve been delving into aerial/drone photography, and of course those lenses are all quite wide and all require a bit of correction.  Overall - this is a solid product and is worth the price of admission. So much so that I bought the lifetime access license after only a week or so of tinkering with it.  Keep up the good work.

The app doesn’t use your on device “Files” to do the editing even though you can import them from there.  I prefer to use an external SSD to save space on my iPad.  Unfortunately, once “imported” into the app it creates a duplicate of all the photos in the Camera roll. And the same goes for all the “albums” in app, it’s actually rearranging them in albums in the default photo album.  It doesn’t sound like a problem until you realize there will either be another duplicate of every exported edited image right next to the original image. If you plan on uploading your exported photos to a cloud backup like in my case where a client needed them to a specific shared Google photos album for example. I think there should be a more clear indication of how the images will be imported and organized to avoid any confusion, especially if your onsite at something like a convention and are experiencing to easily hand over some quick edits.   If there was also a way to leave all photos in the Files app folder and then a way to export the images sites JPEGs to the files locations that would be a great feature.  That way images can be batch moved and selected to go to any platform.   Like I said in the beginning, the editing is pretty solid and simple which is great for on the go iPad work. Yes! Yes. Ummm. No.. TL;DR: I really, really, really wanted to love Darkroom and make it my primary, if not my only, photo developing and editing app. But I just can’t. It’s too buggy and unpredictable across the three platforms.  I’m currently using Darkroom, RAW Power and Pixelmator Pro and Photo for developing and editing my images, most of which are RAW, taken with my iPhone 13 Pro Max. I love Darkroom’s interface, I love RAW Power’s incredible set of tools and its superb results, and I can’t do without Pixelmator’s Repair and ML tools.  David Addison (Pisicul Meu) reviewed the latest iteration of Darkroom and showed off its tremendous new capabilities. He also pointed out some flaws, but the developers are working hard to correct those. His review made me revisit the app after having abandoned earlier versions of it. Previously, it just didn’t hold up feature-wise or performance-wise to the other two apps. But the latest version brought it in line with the competition.  Darkroom’s UI is the best of all three apps, and its Shadow recovery is top-notch. It provides a nearly identical editing experience across my Mac, iPhone and iPad. Its Histogram is terrific, alerting me when an adjustment I’m making is clipping Whites, Blacks or one or more Colors. The order of its tools from top to bottom mimic a really good RAW development workflow. It has added a basic rating system that is appreciated.   But some quirks remain, and new ones have been introduced. Unlike RP or PP, Darkroom had to abandon its macOS Photos Edit Extension. They acknowledge a macOS bug that they blame on Apple that messes with window states when the app is closed but not quit, a bug that the competition doesn’t suffer from. If I try to share an image from some third party camera apps to Darkroom on my iPhone, Darkroom simply will not launch. The competition does. Other third party apps and the native iOS camera app *do* manage to call Darkroom and have it launch successfully. Darkroom’s TIFF export is limited compared to the competition. Darkroom has no auto functions other than LUTs/Looks to give me a head start on adjusting my photos. Darkroom’s metadata display is limited compared to the other two apps. And so on. I’ve run into other annoyances and inconsistencies, enough so that I want to wait a year or so before I revisit Darkroom again.  Let me end this by saying that for a lot of users (and maybe most of them), Darkroom is an outstanding tool that will do everything they need or want. Sadly, I’m not one of them.

This app is flawless. Using it has mostly replaced my use of the standard iOS photos program (the Darkroom thumbnail/photo viewer is that good). The workflow of editing my photos in Darkroom and uploading them to social is as simple as it can be. The three modes of viewing (one full screen, one with control options, one with full controls) navigate with a single swipe.  The actual controls provided are (mostly) standard—this is exactly what I want. Brightness, contrast, clarity—presented so clearly on the screen that for a second I forget to pay attention to the interface. The stickiness of the sliders around their zero is finally usable! It's perfect—the sensitivity adjusts depending on your touch/roll speed to make minor adjustments possible. Getting back to zero is easy. Some innovation around luminance/hue/saturation is nicely provided.  The default presets are demure and appropriate starting points. Managing custom presets is straightforward.  Options are presented clearly when necessary—mostly through a non-hierarchical "..." menu. This is important—it makes things easier to find! The right set of choices is presented—this is part of why I say this app is flawless. Being able to *perfectly* do what I *needed* to do becomes light and fun.  The app doesn't provide cloud storage—but it doesnt need to. I am also a fan of other coloring and filtering programs out there (which do provide cloud storage). What I have gotten switching to Darkroom is an improved (simpler) workflow, without app-supplied cloud storage (and better for it) and the coloring options presented more clearly (as clearly as I have ever seen).  As a result I tend to color in a more straightforward way (than when I had AI-suggested presets)—and I color more happily. Having just the right options presented wonderfully is a major part of why Darkroom has become a Swiss Army Knife-level tool—simple, perfect, deadly.  In my pocket for the foreseeable.  ▵dirt

And is too buggy and slow to recommend at all. I want to love this app, I really do. But as it stands now it falls frustratingly short. Its incredibly buggy, slow, and lacks some features that it really should have at this price point. On that note, price. This app is overpriced, and does not offer the features you’d expect at this price point. For the price this app is being sold for, it is competing with Adobe Lightroom. This app does not even come close to Lightroom. No custom curves, no noise removal, no custom masks. All of this is missing. You get the most basic touchup sliders, selective color, some pre-made filters, and linear/radial masks. Just a bit better than the built in iOS photo editing tools To put the price in perspective, you can buy Affinity Photo for iPad 3 times over for the price the permanent license is being sold for. And thats a full fledged Photoshop competitor. Now lets talk about the bugs, because oh boy this app has them. Since theres no good way to submit a bug in-app, I’m just going to list the ones I’ve found here. -Masks CONSTANTLY de-syncing with their control points. Leaving the actual masked area decoupled from the points you drag around to place and size it. -Exporting pictures sometimes just… doesn’t export your edits! Requiring a full app restart. -Edits just not appearing at all until you open up one of the editing tools.  -Generally slow rendering and performance. Even on a maxed out 2021 iPad Pro. You will be waiting a second or two every time you zoom in for the app to re-render the image. On that note: The initial image shown to you when you open a picture is of significantly lower resolution. Making it appear blurry. Zooming in causes the app to re-render the section you zoomed in on, somewhat fixing this but… Thats so clunky and slow. I understand the need for the developers to make money on the thing they pour so much effort into, but the subscription for this app is honestly a joke when you put it up with what it’s competing against. I want apps like this to succeed. To have something that de-thrones Adobe. But this ain’t it.

Nice concept, too-slow execution. While not quite a ghost town, Glass seems to be running on fumes. There are relatively few new images being uploaded into this subscription service, and the engagement is weak. A noticeable number of photographers stopped contributing images a few months ago. Glass seems more a collection of bubbles than an interactive community. The marketing of Glass still seems to be based on what it is not, rather than what it is and what it could be. If Glass was brand new, I’d be more sympathetic, but the feature set is bare bones, which is probably the result of underfunding. Glass could be a photographic community with people exchanging information and insights, yet there are zero forum-type features that bring people together. Glass could have portfolio-oriented viewing environments, yet an artist cannot group images to form projects or sets that tell a larger, deeper story. Tagging of images is not possible, so one cannot search for specific equipment or genres of images besides the rudimentary categories that are provided for all users. This all feels very 1995-ish. The inability of the developers to make tangible improvements in the app’s scope is especially sad because the opportunity is even greater now than when the app debuted in August 2021: Instagram is dropping photographic still images in favor of a TikTok wannabe approach, and Facebook is making personal timelines secondary to TikTok-like media streams of nonsense. I would think that avoiding the overhead of advertising, customer data mining, and algorithm engineering would enable a more nimble way of working. This Glass seems too thin to expand to the larger universe.

Expectations Don’t Match Reality. The expectation is that someone has finally done something right and made a beautiful applications that avoids the dark patterns plaguing many social sites. And, perhaps they have.  However, the reality is that upon downloading and first running the app that you see it’s subscription based — and for many folks, that’s a deal breaker I am one of those folks, and no two-week free trial will overcome that.  To many, sign-up, free trial, cancel later is a dark pattern (or at least a dark grey, given the process barriers in finding and canceling subscriptions is not zero). Engaging in a commitment to examine a service is an unwelcome barrier.   The monthly subscription rate is along the lines of what one could get their own hosting service for with a little shopping around. Even Apple’s iCloud provides a ton of storage and sleek photo sharing capabilities. So the costs here are more for what you want to put in front of strangers …who also would be willing to pay to see your photos.   Here’s how the app might alter its perception and draw a larger base.  Ideally, upon loading glass you’d be able to see a feed of photos — viewing ought to be free. Commenting ought to require registration for accountability. And posting photos should have some cost (maybe your first 14 are free).  This would grow the community of visitors and that community size could be made public knowledge, because the bigger that number, the more the service is worth.  Simply put, tease us with what you have. Let us show something neat on your feeds to put friends and hook them in as well. And let us start contributing to the community after we feel it’s suitable, appropriate, and non-toxic.   Still, I’d rather see a fixed price app, even one with a higher app price that compensates the developers for their work. The authors are correct that ads ruin app experiences.  Given alternative low-cost high-storage solutions the subscription rate if to cover storage of photos seems absurdly high, more so when one considers the issue in aggregate.  In the end, the Return on Investment (ROI) to post even a few hundred photos a year to a walled garden, which [rightly so] emphasizes shelf-life, doesn’t appear to be worth the ongoing cost of drilling another hole in the wallet.  I intend to revisit in 6mo to see where this app and its community have evolved. I’d like nothing more than to see it fill the application space where Tumblr, Instagram, Flickr, and 500px have failed or ignored.

Terrible Photo Backup App. The primary purpose of a backup is to restore data from it. However, in practice, Immich is horrible at restoring photos to your phone. Consider this scenario: you purchase a new iPhone and use your own Immich server to back up your old iPhone’s photos. You want some of those photos on your new iPhone, so you open the Immich app, connect it to your new phone, and press the download button on a few photos to create a wallpaper on your new iPhone. Surprisingly, the app is coded so poorly that it doesn’t exclude the photos you restored or downloaded from Immich to your new phone. As a result, you end up with duplicates on the Immich server when the auto-backup begins from your new iPhone. It only excludes those photos once it backs them up again.  I conducted some research and discovered that someone had submitted a feature request on the Immich GitHub to “Prevent re-upload of downloaded photos during app backup task.” The maintainer, bo0tzz, responded to them by suggesting that you should exclude the download album from your backup selection. However, this solution is invalid. Once you exclude the download album, you won’t be able to backup any photos saved from Safari or any other app. The app is stupidly designed to only exclude photos it backs up rather than also excluding the restored photos you download from it.

Adobe’s response to the entire situation was even more disappointing.   I despised the change, and it severely disrupted my content creation. Photography was quite honestly one of the few sources of joy in my life amid my health issues, and Lightroom went from being what made me fall in love with photography even more, to the thing that killed what little joy I got to experience in the middle of back-to-back medical treatments.   I cancelled my subscription and don’t see myself using it again.

Very comprehensive. I’ve used Lightroom AI on perhaps a dozen photos of birds captured by a bird feeder camera in my backyard. In AI mode, I find it to be quite good at identifying the various elements present in the photo, such as sky, water, architecture, artificial surfaces, etc., and then providing me with specific editing options which are only performed on that particular element - such changing the blue tone of the water, the saturation or contrast of just the image of the bird itself, etc.   It also has an erasing function that does a significantly better job than the iOS Photo app at replacing a part of the photo I’d like removed. Take the edge of the white plastic feeding tray that the bird is eating out of, which is essentially impossible to avoid being included in a photo. The AI is quite good at replacing the portion I highlight with something that looks like whatever is next to or behind the tray, such as plants or water, if it appears that what’s behind the white tray is our swimming pool. I was very impressed with the app’s ability to intelligently determine what might be seen or revealed if the unwanted part of the native photo weren’t there.  All in all, I find Lightroom AI to be a definite step up from what Apple’s iOS Photo app can do, which is pretty good itself.  My primary embarisingly disappointment and frustration is that the Help or Guides that are supposed to explain and demonstrate what so many of the more advanced tools do and how to use them, are embarrassingly poor and confusing, or don't exist.

Seriously would not recommend. I had really high hopes and expectations for this company, considering that they claim to be #1. I don’t mean to be picky, but last time I checked, number 1 means good quality. That was not the result I saw with this company. The one good thing they did was reprint my order many times—because there were SO many errors. Terrible binding, ink splotches on photos, saturation changes without my request and/or knowledge, etc. If there’s an issue you could imagine with a photo book, I can almost guarantee I had it. And no, it wasn’t me, for example: I used the app to design the book, the text got cut off. I had it reprinted, there were ink splotches. I had it reprinted, the photos were way darker. I had it reprinted again and text was cut off. I saw glue in the binding because it was so poor. I know there is a person out there, maybe creative like me, who really wants to make a keepsake that will be worth anything out into it—please don’t use this company to do so. It’s hard to find other companies with as many reviews or claimed credentials, I get it, that’s true. But good quality shouldn’t come down to luck with a company, it should come down to basic standard control. This is not a professional company, this is one that either has too many products to keep track of, or for lack of a better way to phrase it, has stopped caring about quality control. Make your own pdf, and try to find another company. I don’t think they’ll really miss your book in the non-proof read machines anyway. I don’t want to come off like a typical “1 star” customer, I want to show my experience for someone who wants honesty and care for their time and efforts. Don’t use this company, I hope this review helps. Thanks for reading.

In a different ballpark to other image managers. I’ve searched extensively for a suitable image database app since my first iPad in 2010. They’ve all been inadequate but every year or so I look again. Mylio is the first quality app I’ve found in this space, and I almost missed it. It didn’t come up in any search on the App Store, or on Google, and its logo gave no indication of what it was for. In fact the logo’s lacklustre design led me to suspect it would be yet another mediocre app. I found it at the end of another fruitless search amongst the ‘similar apps’ at the bottom of another app’s page. It’s only because I’m stupidly thorough that I thought I’d try it, expecting more disappointment. But after a week or so’s testing I can say it’s delivered more than my withered expectations dared hope for. Its feature list is full and its implementation both imaginative and disciplined. It has graceful attention to detail while maintaining global consistency and focus. A little familiarisation is required to discover some of the subtler UI elements, but once they’re found they feel practical and intuitive, rather than an opaque indulgence. Only a few apps achieve this balance and quality; I hope whoever’s behind Mylio finds its development rewarding enough to continue because they have some rare skills. Because the app is free for a certain level of usage a general, raving, ‘thumbs up’ is enough comment to encourage new users to explore Mylio’s particular good qualities for themselves. For the devs I’ll mention a couple of specifics that need looking at:  No ‘smart albums’ (populated by keyword associations for example) - UPDATE - the devs say these are coming :-) No quick way to select several images and view them all together free from any others. This is my main criticism, I almost docked a star because if this. People using an app like this are surely heavily invested in their images. Being able to quickly focus in and compare different combinations of images is a common need in such people. - UPDATE - this is being considered by the devs. Folder tree view: being able to visually search and see which folders are nested in which other folders, without having to rely entirely upon memory or go down lots of blind alleys, would be very useful. Keywords: ‘autocomplete’ for keywords which have already been used on other images and a keyword library with the capacity to group keywords into categories would be big time savers.  UPDATE: I’ve docked a star because Mylio does not have import options for the camera roll, only ‘sync’ options. They name sync as import, but images remain linked to the roll and if images are deleted from the roll Mylio only retains preview images in that device’s library, even if those images are moved to a different folder. And because they’re mis-labeling this sync, you may delete the originals thinking they’re safe in Mylio only to lose them altogether. Blown away.. Not to be dramatic but this app has changed my life. By making it effortless to enjoy and rediscover moments from the past and recent times as well—from any of my devices. I’m really poor at taking time to review apps, so I’ll make this one count...  Mylio has flown under the radar and these developers deserve all the praise I can muster.  I’m honestly blown away at how it delivers on all they promise. I’m using it on multiple iPhones, a Mac, iPad, and some external drives as vaults (so far).   I glean and clean up all the albums and photos from my iPhone and all the changes are reflected in the master vault back on the desktop computer at home (a Mac in my case). It can also auto archive your phone camera’s camera roll. This feature is killer.   All my wife’s photos and mine and all the photos and videos from our DSLR cameras  are also constantly in sync and accessible  from any device. This is incredibly hard to promise but they’ve pulled it off.  Mylio is solving for what many wanted iCloud Photo Library to be when that first came out. Then Apple added Family Sharing and shared storage quotas to iCloud a few years ago they still never let people in a “family” really share one library. Even now with iOS 13, not a peep from them on that concept.   Mylio is different and in my view better than most photo hosting tools—because they don’t host. Instead they put all their development effort into making the best photo organizer/discovery/management app and focus on synchronizing between your own devices. You can elect to backup to a 3rd party cloud service or to any of your own backup drives or both. This approach is even more robust and FAR more flexible with options for storage locations and is even cross platform.  SPEED And the performance is impressively fast thus far in a humble set of <25,000 images and video clips thus far. I don’t even think about how fast it is, I just use it and it works as fast as you need it to. Even the UX to me as a new user is really polished. Quite intuitive for such a complex app.

Stunning. This is what Lightroom Mobile should be - no more of this janky "pick a bunch of photos, create a collection, upload photos to Creative Cloud, download photos to your device" etc. With Mylio, you just point the desktop app at your photos, it picks up all of your Lightroom edits and metadata, and your entire photo collection becomes available on all of your devices. And not just one Lightroom catalog, either (unlike Adobe's app) - the photos can be across as many catalogs as you like, it doesn't care (since it's not reading the catalogs themselves, just the RAW/jpeg files and associated XMPs). Mylio even does some editing, with more capabilities being added.  I currently have almost 90,000 photos synced via Mylio across my 5k iMac, iPhone, iPad mini 4, and iPad Pro, and it does this without taking up all of your storage space - you tell it how much free space to leave on the device, and it handles everything in the background, downloading from other devices whatever version of a photo it needs on the fly as you request it. Pretty magical on a fast network.  Any photographer who is paying for Creative Cloud or even just using the retail version of Lightroom should be using Mylio - it will give you an entirely new view into your photo catalog, and will liberate you from your desk (or laptop). Imagine sitting in a comfy chair and having easy access to every photo you've ever taken, being able to search your whole library or filter just one folder via several criteria (keywords, color codes, star ratings, flags, etc), and being able to send any photo to your camera roll for further editing, or straight to Messages, Mail, or social media for immediate sharing.  An extra bonus: Mylio support is responsive and patient, even with a noobie like me who is using the free 30-day trial.

Good editing, poor file / catalog management (vs photoshop). Starting with the good, I moved over from Lightroom after the ridiculous subscription price increases. As an amateur photographer, Lightroom was no longer justifiable.  From an editing perspective, Photomator has several of the basics done well. However, some of the keyboard shortcuts present in Lightroom are missing, such as toggling overlays and quickly inverting settings via shortcuts, which is frustrating. Additionally, features like Compare mode in Lightroom are missing, so I’ve had to use an external program to achieve what I could previously do in one application.  Perhaps the most frustrating thing about this application is how poor library catalogue file management is compared to Lightroom. There is no easy way to import and avoid duplicates, even when I use the inbuilt image capture software in Apple - again a separate program, when LR included this. On top of that, sorting photos in a file by the date it was created in the file’s metadata (EXIF information) is not possible. It seems to register a creation date that is the import date, whereas other files read the EXIF data. This means I cannot view a folder in ascending or descending order by date captured. This is a really basic library navigation feature.  All in all, I’m glad this app exists, but there are some big gaps. I hope the team addresses the file catalogue issues, import issues, and makes keyboard shortcuts and sorting photos by EXIF metadata faster for people who want this kind of programme. I think that’s basic.

The contender has finally arrived. The contender has finally arrived on the iOS iPad scene. A true godsend to photographers where Adobe Lightroom used to dominate. The options provided are plenty. Photomator allows you more freedom in color grading. The HSL adjustment panel is not exclusive to the entire image alone. Each mask has its own HSL adjustment panel where changing one color’s hue, saturation and lightness affects the selected mask area and not the entire image. Especially great where sunset oranges can be adjusted in a specific area without having the image look like it’s been rummaging in a bag of Cheetos. Each individual mask can have its own lut adjustment or preset. The temperature adjustment controls render a better warmer image and vice versa. Other apps fail to enhance warmth without having images turn yellowish. The upscaling option is more than I can describe. Images are upscaled with ease and minimal quality loss. I was able to turn my old Canon 7D 16 megapixel photos to 45 megapixels. My Canon R5 images magically turn into 60 megapixel wonders. With ease.   Two options are currently missing which are Dehaze and the option to choose a rectangular marquee, in which is absent in  Lightroom as well.   I’m glad I’ve jumped ship and will not renew my Lightroom subscription.

Nice photo editor, missing a few odd features. I had been a long time Aperture user before it was discontinued. Tried Lightroom, but always found I wasn’t using it enough to justify the price.   I stumbled across Photomator almost by accident, and am very happy I did. It has some powerful editing tools, retaining some of the DNA of Aperture in my opinion, at a fraction of the price of Lightroom. I can edit photos directly in my Photos library (though I am not sure I would recommend this) or in the file system like you would with a more conventional photo editor.  The issues I have are with a lack of support for some basic features I have come to expect at this point.  1) No EXIF editing. Was your DSLR’s clock wrong? Too bad, no way to fix it here. 2) No geotagging. This was a nice feature in Aperture, I use it extensively in Photos, not present here. 3) No red eye removal. An odd one, because while cell phones have gotten pretty good at dealing with this I feel that DSLRs with flashes are still hit or miss.  4) Lack of feature parity with Photos app. Particularly when it comes to editing iPhone photos, again it just does not have the options you would expect. No DOF editing, no Styles editing. You’re frankly better off sticking with Photos unless you just shoot ProRAW. 5) Sidecar files. This is a big one: to make non-destructive edits, Photomator needs to generate sidecar files to go with every photo. If these get lost or de-coupled, your edits are gone. But worse IMO, depending on your edits these can become truly enormous, many times the size of the original photo. This is why I would not recommend using this to edit an iCloud Photos library directly; these sidecar files will opaquely live in the background and just eat up your storage.   Overall, I’m very happy with this app, especially for the price. However, I have to acknowledge after a few months of use that it is still leaves some holes in an otherwise good photo editing workflow.

Buggy, Useless Magic Eraser, and No Generative AI.. Photomator is not a valid replacement for a program as robust as Adobe Lightroom for three reasons. The first is, the O hotkey to reveal and hide a mask overlay doesn’t work reliably—no matter what settings you toggle on or off. This is a big one, and a serious hindrance during editing that has no workaround. It’s a stupid issue that should not exist. Second, the “magic eraser” that the Pixelmator team likes to tout as an end-all-be-all for removing distracting objects from photos is one of many definitions for garbage. All it does is smear a shoddy jumble of pixels overtop the user’s mask. It doesn’t hide anything, and is so obviously ineffective that no serious photographer could ever trust it to do what it is advertised to do. Lastly, neither Photomator nor Pixelmator has access to generative AI to PROPERLY remove objects from photos. Photomator’s best answer to this is problem is adequate healing tools and great cloning tools that work at the pixel-level to fill in spaces on the user’s canvas as needed. But, those options are not efficient nor are they competitive in today’s market. I really wanted to like this app given how well optimised it is for use on MacOS, but it simply doesn’t do enough to justify leaving behind big industry players. Look elsewhere.

Professional Photographer Review. I have come to use many different programs in my creative endeavors but in terms of photo editing this app is becoming my favorite. The existing features are extremely useful when I need more ability than Apple Photos affords but not as much bloat as what comes with Affinity Photo or Pixelmator (love those apps too by the way).   The features that the developers are working on are also highly useful to the professional photographer.  The automated batch processing feature or “workflows” is perhaps the best feature about Photomator because of the incredible potential to save time. The results are extremely close and it does appear that the program is learning my editing style, though this could just be coincidence. This is a feature that I would LOVE LOVE LOVE to see fully developed and refined.   THERE IS ROOM FOR IMPROVEMENT HOWEVER.  It seems that there are some edits that cannot be automatically applied through this process. This makes the AI editing feature feel new and unrefined. It would be nice to be able to add any editing feature or tool in the program to an automated “Workflow” for automatic processing.   ALSO More ability to control the decisions the AI is making on each photo would make the automatic workflows feature perfect. For example it would be useful to be able to tell the AI to pull shadows up a little more across jobs, or asking it to limit highlights to a certain level that may not be what the AI considers “technically perfect”.  Making the aforementioned upgrades would likely make this app the premier photo editing app for America and maybe the world. Speaking solely for myself, If these changes were made this would become my primary photo editing program since every feature I would need would be in one program that actually saves me time.   Any cons aside, this app is comparable to light room but actually has an ethical price model and is already wildly powerful for its price point. Thank you to the developers! Please keep Photomator going in the amazing direction it is going!

Do not rely on this if you’re a videographer or content creator. I’m a content creator, videographer and photographer, and here’s why after 6+ years of using this, I’m cancelling my subscription:  - EXPORT QUALITY   Constant bugs aside, despite what VSCO tell you in their overzealous brand responses, videos are substantially reduced in quality. Once exported through vsco they are barely good enough for social media let alone anything else.   I flagged this to VSCO several times over the years, and every time I’m given the same response that either it’s my issue (it’s not) or that ‘they’ve taken onboard my feedback and will address it soon’. I’ve even sent over meta data for videos pre-import and post-export, screenshots, screen recordings and genuinely tried to provide them with as much info as possible to assist them in resolving the issue. What a waste of my time. This was YEARS ago. YEARS. The quality issue has never improved. At most I’ve used a couple of the exported videos on stories, but the rest get deleted and edited in other apps.    - APP BUGS   Most recently, the bugs have made this app virtually unusable. Even if you do want to try video editing in this, expect it to crash, the playback to run like a stop motion and if you’re lucky, all the adjustments sometimes disappear once you’ve gone back to home. Photos are just about bearable, although painfully slow, and exporting now has to be done one at a time otherwise it just never exports.   What used to take 3 minutes bulk exporting took me an excruciating hour last time, as I had to go back and forth between my photos to see that it either hadn’t exported, exported a few random ones in no particular order, or exported the same one 5 times. If you fancy a bonus task of working out what did and didn’t export, deleting duplicates and easily getting into a filing mess in the process - this is the app for you.   - PRESETS AND EDITING  The presets are great though, that really is the only thing VSCO has going for it but even that’s losing value as more apps pop up delivering similar with better performance.   Actual editing however is extremely basic and an app that markets it self to professionals via a subscription would have at least introduced some more tools in the last 5 years. And no, I’m not including that awful ‘remove’ tool that’s been in beta mode for over a year and will only make your photos worse. Honestly, if simple, free face editing apps can nail a healing tool, VSCO should be able to quite easily.   - OVERALL    If you’re a content creator or SMM, you might get away with editing some videos on this and using them on stories, but even there you’ll see a drop in quality. I wouldn’t recommend for reels, even when just editing phone footage because the result is awful. I can always tell when someone’s reel has been edited in VSCO because of its tale-tale compression signs.      If you’re an amateur photographer, love the presets, and don’t mind limited features and a chaotic and slow workflow, you might be the only person this app works for. Although there are much better alternatives available now that are both cheaper and less buggy and the presets are AMAZING.   If you’re a videographer, don’t even waste your time. You’ll likely end up with a really beautifully edited video in the VSCO app, using a gorgeous preset and lots of fine tuning and you’ll love it. And then your heart will sink when you export it and realise it’s totally unusable and only good for the delete button. I would never send a VSCO edited video to a client for this reason. My work deserves better, and so does yours.   - FINAL WORD  No doubt underneath this will be, or will soon be, VSCOs usual ‘oh no, that’s unusual’ response as if this is a totally isolated issue and they have no idea what’s going on. Perhaps we’ll even see the ‘please contact us with your video specs and we’ll look into this for you because it should be exporting at the same quality’. Spoiler alert - they’re already aware and they don’t care.   So long VSCO!

The best editing app for photographers, not selfieholics. There are many reviews complaining VSCO isn’t free, or that’s it’s ‘boring’, but as a photographer this app is invaluable for tweaking or editing before uploading to socials or photo archive sites. I say this as a ‘real camera’ photographer and someone who had Lightroom and Capture 1 at my disposal.  The preset film styles may not always be spot-on, but that’s mostly due to the original photo than the expertise of the app creators (I still miss their excellent LR presets). But they offer an excellent starting point, and allow the tweaking of characteristics to get the look you want. My favourite are the Fuji simulations. But if even if I’ve edited the photo already in LR, the ability to give it a little tweak, add some grain, crop to 5:4 for Instagram etc, it’s worth the price alone for me as a daily user. And I mustn’t overlook the fact it’s also a social photo gallery app too. You can upload your photos in higher quality than Instagram, and enjoy a more pleasant environment among photographers than the content scraping, tiktok reposting, dumpster that is Instagram. Highly recommend 👍

A beautiful tool that continues to evolve.. Mymind is one of the most elegant and frictionless tools I’ve used for capturing thoughts, inspiration, and media. It feels more like a creative companion than a productivity app—quietly helpful, never overwhelming, and beautifully designed.  The experience of saving things—articles, quotes, images, links—is seamless, and I love how it encourages you to revisit your own ideas through features like Serendipity. You can tell this was made by people who care deeply about both form and function.  That said, I’d love to see the organizational side continue to evolve. While the smart tagging is a great start, I still found myself wishing for a stronger sense of context—like lightweight summaries or relational links between saved items to help me remember why I saved something. Something that nudges memory without adding work.  But overall, this is an incredibly well-crafted tool with a lot of heart and potential. Highly recommended to anyone who wants to think more clearly without the clutter.

Compliments and Feedback. I’ve been using my mind for well over a year and it is genuinly one of my favourite apps out there. However I do have some constructive criticism.  First, please allow for more ‘space’ colour rings, more customisation options would be nice as I’ve run out of rings already!  Second, is there no “multiple cards” selection? I find it difficult to have to slowly pick out single cards to put them all into a space at one time, or select multiple cards to tag them at once.   Lastly, is there an option to view duplicate cards? I feel I’ve had two of the same card but they’re so far apart I struggle to remember. Does this option exist in the other subscriptions or does this not exist? If so I’d love it!  Overall, I do love this app but there are definitely some updates needed.

A fleeting memory no longer debilitates my progress; every passing thought (or 2am rabbit hole I’ve gone down) is visually recorded there.
